title: Sales Enablement: Unified Playbook — Positioning, Competitive Briefs, Pitch Decks, Pricing Guidance, Case Studies & Security FAQ
author: Asha Patel
body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook consolidates the core sales enablement artifacts necessary for pre-sales and account teams to position Redwood Inference, defend value vs. competitors, deliver consistent pitch decks, discuss pricing and contracting levers, present short case studies, and answer common prospect security questions. Use this document as the single source of truth for go-to-market collateral and update the referenced assets (deck, battlecards, price sheet) when changes are approved.

Audience: AEs, Solutions Engineers, Customer Success, Sales Leadership, Channel Partners.

Key takeaways (elevator pitches)

- Developer / Platform buyer: "Redwood Inference gives your engineering team a unified runtime and observability for LLM inference so you can ship reliable, low-latency features without owning the full serving stack."
- Product / PM buyer: "We help you deliver predictable UX and controllable unit economics for LLM features — letting you trade cost, latency, and quality with measurable levers."
- Security / Compliance buyer: "We support private deployments, customer-managed key options, and audit-grade logging so regulated workloads meet enterprise requirements."

Positioning & Messaging (core pillars)

1) Production-first performance and predictability
- High-throughput serving runtime tuned for modern attention and quantized variants.
- Observable per-token cost and latency. Prescriptive recommendations to reduce unit costs (batching, caching, quantization).

2) Unified runtime across environments
- Same API/SDK, model catalog, and rollout controls across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments — minimizes engineering overhead when moving between modes.

3) Cost-aware controls with transparent economics
- Deterministic levers (batching policies, cache lifetime, quant profiles) with measurable SLO and unit-cost impact.

4) Reliability with graceful degradation
- Smart routing and automatic fallbacks (model variants, regional failover) to keep customer UX available under capacity constraints.

Messaging guidance (by audience)

- Engineering: Lead with API parity, runtime optimizations, and integration examples. Provide latency and throughput benchmarks for comparable workloads.
- Platform teams / infra: Lead with deployment modes (Dedicated vs Private), SLA/commit options, and integration points for KMS, VPC, and telemetry.
- Product/Exec: Focus on unit economics, time-to-market, and risk mitigation (fallbacks, audit logs). Use case metrics in brief.

Competitive brief (high-level)

Competitors covered: Managed LLM API providers, cloud AI endpoints, self-hosted inference runtimes, and niche inference vendors.

Differentiation matrix (summary)

| Dimension | Redwood | Cloud-managed endpoints | LLM API (core competitor) | Self-hosted runtime |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Developer DX | High (SDKs, templates) | Medium | High | Low–Medium |
| Production SLAs | Available (Dedicated) | Variable | Low–Medium | Depends |
| Cost controls | Prescriptive (batching, quant) | Limited | Limited | Potentially high ops cost |
| Private/On‑prem | Yes (Private) | Limited | No | Yes (but you operate it) |
| Observability | Token-level cost + traces | Basic metrics | Basic | Varies |

Defensive talking points vs common competitors

- Against general cloud AI endpoints: "Cloud endpoints provide model access but not the production controls and cost primitives (batching/cache/quantization) you need to operate economically at scale. Redwood gives those controls plus the same API across deployment modes."
- Against LLM API-focused vendors: "Some API vendors prioritize simplicity for prototypes; Redwood focuses on production economics and SLAs for product features, plus private deployment options for regulated customers."
- Against self-hosted runtimes: "Self-hosted can be flexible but is expensive to operate and fragile. Redwood provides an opinionated runtime with operational tooling and SRE expertise built in, reducing time to production and operational burden."

Pitch deck outline (recommended 12–15 slides)

1) Title / Intro — Short mission line and logo
2) Why now — market context for inference economics and model proliferation
3) Customer problems — cost, latency, reliability, ops complexity
4) Redwood solution overview — Hosted, Dedicated, Private (one-liner for each)
5) How it works (high level) — serving runtime, routing, caching, deployment abstraction
6) Developer experience — API, SDKs, quickstarts, model catalog
7) Performance benchmarks — representative latency & throughput charts (include sample data)
8) Cost controls — batching, caching, quantization recommendations (include expected % savings ranges)
9) Reliability & SLAs — Dedicated SLA targets and fallback behaviors
10) Security & compliance — KMS integrations, network isolation, audit logs, certifications
11) Pricing & purchasing options — hosted pricing examples, Dedicated commits, Private enterprise terms
12) Case studies — 2–3 short customer outcomes with metrics
13) Roadmap & support — observability, rollouts, eval tooling
14) Next steps / Call to action — POC, tech deep-dive, pricing worksheet

Speaker notes: Keep slides lean; have an appendix with technical architecture, SLOs and sample configs for SEs to reference during demos. Always pre-populate the deck with the prospect name and a one-slide tailored value statement.

Pricing guidance (principles and sample tiers)

Principles
- Be transparent: show per-token economics and expected savings from recommended optimizations.
- Offer predictable options: reserved capacity (Dedicated) for throughput-sensitive customers.
- Provide enterprise packaging: Private deployments priced as platform fee + support/ops margin + optional on-prem packaging.

Sample pricing guidance (representative only — use final price sheet for negotiation)

| Mode | Pricing model | Typical commitment | Key levers |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Hosted API | Pay-as-you-go (per input token / per output token / per embedding unit) | None | Rate limits, quotas, model selection |
| Dedicated | Monthly reserved GPU pool (commit) + overage | 3–12 months | Autoscale burst, commit size, SLA tier |
| Private | Enterprise license + support + deployment services | 12+ months | Integration scope, compliance add-ons |

Negotiation and discounting guidance

- Early-stage/startups: emphasize Hosted trials and credits, small discounts for marketing/case-study commitments.
- Mid-market: typical 5–15% discount on committed Dedicated capacity depending on term & payment terms.
- Strategic enterprise: negotiate platform fee, integration services, professional services credits, and multi-year discounts. Tie larger discounts to longer terms and larger commit sizes.

Contract levers to offer

- Commit size / term length
- SLA level (economy vs enterprise)
- Observability retention window (longer retention = higher price)
- Managed ops add-ons (SRE-run Dedicated)

Case studies (condensed)

1) FinTech customer — realtime guidance assistant
- Problem: High latency and unbounded inference cost causing poor user experience and margin pressure.
- Solution: Migrated to Redwood Dedicated with prefix caching and model variant routing.
- Outcome: 45% reduction in per-query cost, 30% lower median latency, throughput scaled to 10k QPS during peak.

2) SaaS productivity company — summarization & search embeddings
- Problem: Growing cost from embedding calls and inconsistent quality across model versions.
- Solution: Use Redwood Optimize to recommend quantization profile and per-route caching; pinned model versions and rollout policy.
- Outcome: 60% reduction in embedding unit cost, eliminated regressions through staged rollouts.

3) Regulated healthcare customer — private deployment
- Problem: Data residency and audit requirements prevented cloud-hosted models.
- Solution: Private deployment with customer-managed KMS and audit log forwarding to SIEM.
- Outcome: Successful SOC2/ISO audits for the workload, enabled product launch for HIPAA-adjacent customers.

Security FAQ for prospects (concise answers for common questions)

Q: Where does customer data reside?
A: Hosted data is stored in region-specific clusters per customer selection. Dedicated pools are logically isolated; Private deployments keep data in customer VPC/on‑prem as specified in the contract.

Q: How is data encrypted?
A: Data is encrypted in transit (TLS 1.2+) and at rest (AES-256). For Hosted/Dedicated we support customer-managed keys via KMS integrations; Private deployments can integrate with customer HSMs.

Q: Do you persist request logs and prompts?
A: By default we persist audit logs and metrics necessary for billing and troubleshooting. For sensitive customers we offer configurable retention windows and options to disable prompt retention in Private deployments.

Q: What compliance certifications do you hold?
A: Redwood maintains SOC2 Type II. We provide evidence packages for enterprise audits and have a roadmap for ISO27001. For regulated workloads we engage our compliance team to provide attestation and required documentation.

Q: How do you support access control and RBAC?
A: We integrate with SSO providers (SAML/OIDC) and provide fine‑grained role-based access controls in the Console and API keys. We log admin actions for auditability.

Q: What is your incident response and disclosure policy?
A: We follow our incident response runbook with customer notifications aligned to severity and SLA. We publish an incident postmortem to affected customers and offer dedicated communication channels for enterprise accounts.

Q: How are third-party dependencies managed?
A: We maintain an approved vendor list, perform regular security reviews, and require critical vendors to meet our security controls. Pen tests are performed annually and after major releases; results are available under NDA.

Enablement playbooks & checklists (SE checklist for initial meetings)

1) Pre-call: Review account profile, target use-case, likely deployment mode, and security profile. Load the tailored deck.
2) Discovery: Confirm SLAs, throughput needs, data sensitivity, and integration constraints (KMS, VPC, SIEM).
3) Demo: Show API quickstart, latency metrics, SDK code snippets, and the Console for per-route cost breakdown.
4) Follow-up: Share sample pricing worksheet, proposed POC scope, and security questionnaire answers.

Assets and templates to attach

- Pitch deck (editable): sales/pitch-deck-redwood-inference-2026.pptx
- Price worksheet: sales/price-worksheet-redwood-2026.xlsx
- SE battlecard: sales/battlecards/llm-inference-battlecard-2026.pdf
- Case study one-pagers: marketing/case-studies/*
- Security FAQ (detailed): security/security-faq-detailed-2026.pdf (NDA required)

Ownership and update process

- Owner: Sales Enablement (go-to-market). Content steward: Asha Patel.
- Review cadence: Quarterly for messaging and after major product or price changes.
- Approval: Changes to pricing or security claims must be approved by Product and Security leadership respectively before publication.

Appendix: Example technical config snippets

    -H 'Authorization: Bearer <KEY>'
    -d '{"model":"redwood-llm-v1","input":"Summarize the following...","max_tokens":256}'

- Example Dedicated SLA summary:
  - Uptime: 99.95%
  - Target p50 latency: 50ms for 512-token contexts
  - Support: 24x7 critical on-call for enterprise tiers
